title: Course Schedule — Topological Sort & Cycle Detection
prompt: There are numCourses labeled 0..numCourses-1. You're given prerequisites where prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means you must take course b before course a. First: return whether you can finish all courses (i.e., is it possible to complete every course given the prerequisites?). Follow-up: return a valid ordering of courses to take; return an empty array if it's impossible.
blurb: A dependency graph where 'can you finish?' is exactly 'is this graph a DAG?' — topological sort via Kahn's BFS or DFS cycle detection.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Models courses as nodes and prerequisites as directed edges; recognizes 'can finish' <=> 'no cycle' <=> 'graph is a DAG'. Clarifies edge direction.

rubric.label: Approach
rubric.description: Chooses Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degrees) or DFS with three-color cycle detection; can articulate both.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: Builds adjacency + in-degrees correctly for the b->a direction; detects a cycle (processed count < numCourses, or gray-node revisit) and returns the right result.

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: O(V + E) time and O(V + E) space; explains why building the graph and each traversal are linear in nodes+edges.

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: Clean adjacency-list build, in-degree array, a queue seeded with zero-in-degree nodes; no quadratic re-scans.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: No prerequisites (all independent), self-loop [a,a], duplicate edges, disconnected components, a simple 2-course cycle.

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Tests a cyclic case and a valid-order case, and checks a disconnected/no-prereq case.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: States the DAG framing up front and explains why processed-count < numCourses means a cycle.

constraints: Edges may be duplicated; watch for self-loops [a,a] which are trivially cyclic

examples.explanation: Take 0 first (no prereqs), then 1. No cycle, so all courses finishable.
0 requires 1 and 1 requires 0 — a cycle. Neither can start, so it's impossible.

reference.optimal_space: O(V + E) for the adjacency list, in-degree array, and queue/stack

approaches.name: brute force (repeated removal)
approaches.idea: Repeatedly scan for a course with all prereqs satisfied, remove it, and repeat until stuck or done. Correct but re-scans the whole set each round.

approaches.name: optimal A: Kahn's algorithm (BFS topological sort)
approaches.idea: Build adjacency list (b -> a for each [a,b]) and an in-degree array. Seed a queue with all zero-in-degree nodes. Repeatedly pop a node, append to the order, and decrement each neighbor's in-degree, enqueuing any that hit zero. If the number of processed nodes equals numCourses, there's no cycle (return true / the order); otherwise a cycle exists (return false / []).

approaches.name: optimal B: DFS with three-color cycle detection
approaches.idea: DFS each unvisited node coloring nodes white(unvisited)/gray(in current stack)/black(done). Encountering a gray node during DFS means a back edge => cycle. Push nodes to a stack on finish; the reverse of finish order is a valid topological order. A self-loop is caught as an immediate gray hit.

follow_ups: Return a valid ordering (Course Schedule II) — Kahn's produces it directly as the dequeue order.
Return ALL valid topological orderings (backtracking over zero-in-degree choices) — exponential, discuss when it's acceptable.
Minimum number of semesters if you can take unlimited courses in parallel each semester with satisfied prereqs — BFS by 'levels' of the DAG (longest-path / level count).
Detect and report the actual cycle (the set of courses involved), not just its existence.
Streaming/incremental: prerequisites arrive over time — maintain whether the graph stays acyclic (incremental cycle detection).
reference.reference_solution: Build graph: adj = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]; indeg = [0]*numCourses. For each [a,b] in prerequisites: adj[b].append(a); indeg[a]+=1  (edge b->a: b before a). Kahn's: queue = all nodes with indeg==0; order=[]. While queue: node=queue.pop(); order.append(node); for nxt in adj[node]: indeg[nxt]-=1; if indeg[nxt]==0: queue.append(nxt). If len(order)==numCourses: return true (or order); else return false (or []). The count check IS the cycle test: nodes stuck in a cycle never reach in-degree 0, so they're never processed. For Course Schedule I just return the boolean; for II return order when complete else []. Getting the edge direction right ([a,b] means b before a, so the edge points b->a and a's in-degree increases) is the most common correctness slip.
pitfalls: Reversing the edge direction — building a->b instead of b->a inverts the whole ordering.
Forgetting that processed-count < numCourses is the cycle signal (not throwing an exception or looping forever).
Not handling self-loops [a,a], which are immediate cycles.
In the DFS version, using a single 'visited' boolean instead of three colors — you'll miss back edges or falsely flag cross edges.
Re-scanning all nodes each round (the O(V^2) brute force) on large inputs.

interviewer_notes: Listen for the framing 'can I finish' == 'is this a DAG / is there a cycle?' — that reframing is the whole insight and should come early. If they don't graph-model it, ask 'what does it mean, in graph terms, that you can't finish?' The most common bug is edge direction; when they build the adjacency list, quietly confirm with them what [1,0] means and let them self-correct if reversed. Kahn's is usually the cleaner answer here because it yields the ordering for the follow-up for free — if they do DFS, ask them to also produce a valid order and check they reverse the finish-order stack. Once canFinish is correct, escalate to Course Schedule II (return the order), then the 'minimum semesters with parallelism' variant, which requires level-BFS thinking and separates mid from senior.
